title: "Week 10 Self-Check"
subtitle: "MC 501 · The Sample and the Pilot"
---

Eight questions on this week's terms. **Nothing here is graded and nothing is recorded.** Answer
each question in your head or on paper first, then open the answer under it.

Every term is defined on the slides: [Week 10, The Sample and the Pilot](../decks/mc501/w10-sample-pilot.html).
Variables, mediators, and moderators are explained in
[Chapter 5](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v/chapters/chapter05.html#variables-the-building-blocks-of-hypotheses),
and sampling and reliability in [Chapter 10](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v/chapters/chapter10.html).

## 1. Independent and dependent variables

Hypothesis: "Non-gaming streams draw a higher share of chat messages aimed at the streamer than
gaming streams do." Which is the **independent variable (IV)** and which is the **dependent
variable (DV)**?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 1</summary>

The **IV** is stream type, gaming or non-gaming: the proposed cause. The **DV** is the share of
chat messages aimed at the streamer: the outcome you think stream type changes. Both are
**variables** because each can change from one case to the next.

</details>

## 2. A mediator

A researcher argues that non-gaming streams feel more like a conversation, and that this feeling
is what invites viewers to message the streamer. What role does "feels like a conversation" play?

- **A.** Independent variable
- **B.** Dependent variable
- **C.** Mediator
- **D.** Moderator

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 2</summary>

**C, a mediator.** A mediator sits in the middle and explains how or why the IV changes the DV:
stream type, then the conversational feel, then messages to the streamer.

</details>

## 3. A moderator

The link between stream type and messages to the streamer holds on small streams and fades on
large ones. What role does audience size play?

- **A.** Independent variable
- **B.** Dependent variable
- **C.** Mediator
- **D.** Moderator

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 3</summary>

**D, a moderator.** A moderator changes how strong the IV's effect is, or its direction. It
answers "under what conditions?" Audience size does not sit between stream type and the outcome;
it changes how strongly the two are linked.

</details>

## 4. Population, sampling frame, and the gap

You plan to study every post in one subreddit during 2025. You collect posts through a search tool
that skips deleted posts. Name the **population**, the **sampling frame**, and one **gap**.

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 4</summary>

The **population** is every post in that subreddit during 2025. The **sampling frame** is the list
of posts the search tool actually returns. One **gap** is the deleted posts, which belong to the
population but never reach the frame. Your Sampling Plan states all three in writing.

</details>

## 5. Sampling for a moderator

You expect audience size to moderate the effect of stream type. How should you draw your sample?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 5</summary>

**Stratify by audience size**, so small streams and large streams both appear in the sample. A
simple random draw of messages would come mostly from the busiest channels and leave too few small
streams to see the moderator at work. To test a moderator, the sample needs cases at every level
of it.

</details>

## 6. The seed

Why does `seed = 409` matter when you draw your sample?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 6</summary>

A **seed** fixes a random draw so it comes out the same on every run. The number itself is
arbitrary; what matters is that a seed is set and recorded in your plan. Without it, nobody can
reproduce your sample or check your results, including you.

</details>

## 7. Raw agreement and kappa

Your two passes give the same code on 74 of 100 items, but **Cohen's kappa** comes out at 0.236.
What does that tell you?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 7</summary>

**Most of the agreement was luck.** Chance agreement alone would have been about 66 percent, and
kappa credits the codebook only with agreement beyond chance. A value of 0.236 is well under 0.70,
so the codebook needs its unclear rules repaired and a fresh pilot.

</details>

## 8. Kappa or alpha

Three coders rate how heated each message is on a scale from 1 to 5, and a few items are missing a
code. Should you report Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha?

<details class="tmpl-section"><summary>Show the answer to question 8</summary>

**Krippendorff's alpha.** Kappa is built for two sets of codes and **nominal** categories, which
are only names with no order. Alpha works with any number of coders, with ranked or numeric codes
such as a 1 to 5 scale, and with missing codes.

</details>
